issues.legal_issue: A court has inherent jurisdiction to address a decree obtained by fraud, and res judicata does not protect a judgment so obtained.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, a preliminary decree recognized the mortgagor’s sisters as having shares in the property.

The appellant challenged the decree, relying on documents indicating that the sisters had no interest and alleging that material facts, including their father’s death before the applicable succession law came into force, had been suppressed.

The High Court set aside an order allowing the challenge on the ground that the procedural provisions invoked did not empower the court to set aside the preliminary decree for fraud, and relied on earlier orders to bar the challenge.
issues.conclusion: The court has inherent jurisdiction to address a decree obtained by fraud, including under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. If fraud on the court is established, res judicata does not apply; the High Court erred in shutting out the challenge on that basis, and its judgment was set aside for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Fraud vitiates judicial acts and cannot be protected by finality or res judicata. Under Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, courts have inherent power to recall or set aside an order obtained by fraud on the court; the absence of an express procedural provision does not eliminate that jurisdiction. The court relied on S.P. Chengalvaraya Naidu v. Jagannath, Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) Pvt. Ltd., Smt. Shrisht Dhawan v. M/s. Shaw Brothers, Lazarus Estates Ltd. v. Beasley, Manohar Lal Chopra v. Rai Bahadur Rao Raja Seth Hiralal, and Sharda v. Dharmpal.

predicates.challenge_to_judicial_decree: A person brought a court proceeding challenging a judicial decree.
predicates.material_facts_concealed_from_court: A party to the proceeding withheld material facts from the court when seeking the decree.
predicates.false_representation_induced_decree: A party made a false representation that induced the court to grant the decree.

issues.definition: When a judicial decree is challenged and material concealment or an inducing false representation is shown, the court may set aside a decree obtained by fraud.

issues.legal_issue: A consent order cannot extinguish an auction purchaser’s third-party rights without consideration of those rights, particularly where the purchaser was not a party to the consent.
material_facts: The appellant purchased property at a court auction, the sale was confirmed, and he took possession before the consent order was made in the first appeal.
The appellant was not a party to that appeal or to the compromise underlying the consent order.
The appellant alleged that the parties to the appeal had not disclosed the auction sale or its confirmation.
The High Court dismissed the appellant’s review application without addressing whether the consent order could affect his rights as auction purchaser.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to consider whether the consent order could set at naught the auction purchaser’s rights, taking account of the sale, its confirmation, and the purchaser’s absence from the appeal and compromise. Its failure to address those matters required the review order to be set aside and the matter reconsidered.
issues.legal_principle: A consent order is an agreement between the parties with the court’s seal superadded, and a third party’s rights cannot be set at naught by consent. A court considering review must address material subsequent events and their effect on third-party rights. The court relied on Dwarka Prasad Agarwal (D) by Lrs. v. B.D. Agarwal and Rajesh D. Darbar v. Narasingrao Krishnaji Kulkarni.

predicates.review_of_consent_order: A person sought review of a court order made by consent of the parties to a proceeding.
predicates.third_party_right_created_before_consent: A court-related transaction created a third party’s right before the consent order was made.
predicates.affected_person_not_party_to_consent: The person whose right may be affected was not a party to the proceeding or the consent.

issues.definition: When review concerns a consent order and a prior-created third-party right of someone who was not party to the consent, the order cannot extinguish that right without the court considering it.

issues.legal_issue: A court must adjust the equities when later events and its own acts affect the parties’ rights, and must not allow unjust enrichment at another party’s expense.
material_facts: The respondents had deposited money pursuant to the consent order, and the State Government had appropriated it.
The auction purchaser’s rights and the consequences of the auction remained unresolved.
The bank’s enforcement of its mortgage decree could result in recovery from the judgment debtors while also leaving the auction purchaser to bear the loss.
The High Court had not addressed the parties’ equities or the effect of the court’s acts and subsequent events.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was required to consider the effect of the fraud allegations and the parties’ conduct, adjust the equities in light of the subsequent events, and avoid unjust enrichment. The matters were remitted for fresh consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Courts may take account of subsequent events and mould relief in exceptional circumstances. The equitable maxim actus curiae neminem gravabit means that an act of the court shall prejudice no person; the court must also avoid unjust enrichment. The court relied on Rajesh D. Darbar v. Narasingrao Krishnaji Kulkarni, Raj Kumar Dey v. Tarapada Dey, Gursharan Singh v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, and Mohammed Gazi v. State of Madhya Pradesh.

predicates.proceeding_to_adjust_equities: A court proceeding requires the court to determine or adjust the parties’ equitable positions.
predicates.subsequent_events_affect_party_rights: Events occurring after the relevant order affected the parties’ rights or the practical consequences of relief.
predicates.court_act_caused_or_risked_prejudice: An act or order of the court caused or risked prejudice to a party.
predicates.enforcement_would_cause_unjust_enrichmen: Enforcing an order in the circumstances would allow one party to obtain an unfair benefit at another party’s expense.

issues.definition: When later events affect rights and a court act risks prejudice or enforcement risks unjust enrichment, the court must adjust the parties’ equities.
